exit_trigger: Evidence that additive customers are switching suppliers or that pricing power has eroded; Long-term demand destruction from engine and fuel technology change that the company cannot offset; Management capital allocation failure, such as large value-destroying acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Debt-to-equity rising meaningfully above 0.5 with no clear path back; Price above 1.5x a conservatively re-derived intrinsic value that persists
rationale: I own this one, and I'm down about 21% on my single share from the $886.815 I paid in August. A lower price, with nothing in the snapshot showing the business has changed, is not a reason to sell. The numbers I can see are good: a 5-year average ROE of 30.6%, owner earnings averaging about $413 million against a $6.57 billion market cap, and a computed margin of safety of 45%. But that valuation rests on an 8% growth cap and a 5% discount rate, which is generous, so I discount it in my own head. Debt-to-equity of 0.497 clears my 0.5 line by a whisker, and I can't verify the 10-year earnings record or management tenure from this snapshot. I'll keep holding, I won't add until I've confirmed those gaps, and the real risk I'm watching is whether the product mix and customer qualifications stay sticky as engines and fuels change.

exit_trigger: Not applicable, no position held; Would revisit only if evidence emerged of a durable, structural pricing or cost advantage and a margin of safety well above 15%
rationale: I understand what Best Buy does. It buys consumer electronics and appliances from a handful of big suppliers and sells them through stores and online. That is exactly the problem: I can't point to a durable moat. The products are the same ones a customer can price-check on a phone, and the suppliers hold much of the brand power. The numbers on the page look good: market cap of about $20.9 billion, a 5-year average ROE of 48.4% and debt-to-equity of 0.39. But the margin of safety is only 15.3%, and the snapshot assumes 0% growth. A thin margin on a business without a moat is not a wonderful company at a fair price, and I'd rather pass and wait for a better pitch. Cheapness alone does not make a business a good one.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand erosion: sustained discounting or loss of pricing power; Management destroys value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Dishonest or opaque communication, or accounting problems; Price persistently above 1.5x a conservatively re-derived intrinsic value; A much higher-conviction opportunity that requires the capital
rationale: I own these shares, bought at $128.38 and now at $111.82, down 12.9%. A lower price with no change in the business is not a reason to sell. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 34.6%, debt-to-equity reported at 0.0, and owner earnings of about $1.32 billion against a $12.35 billion market cap. The model's $346.97 intrinsic value rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on a number that sensitive. Even a heavy haircut leaves a wide margin of safety. So I keep the position at its current size, I don't add until I can check that, and I won't sell just because Mr. Market is glum.

exit_trigger: Evidence that franchise protections are weakening, for example direct-to-consumer manufacturer sales spreading to its brands; Service and parts profitability deteriorating materially over several years; Management making large acquisitions at peak prices or taking on leverage beyond the 0.5 debt-to-equity ceiling; Price rising above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; A far better opportunity at much higher conviction
rationale: I own this one, and the numbers in front of me give me no reason to sell. Five-year average ROE of 23.8% with debt-to-equity of 0.39 is good work for a retailer, and at $212.56 against an owner-earnings value of about $259.62 I get an 18.1% margin of safety, past my 15% bar, using zero growth and a 5% discount rate. But I'll be honest: a car dealer's moat is thinner than Coca-Cola's. It rests on franchise protections and scale, not on a brand in the customer's mind. The snapshot also doesn't give me ten years of earnings, CEO tenure, ROIC or insider activity, so I can't call this a wonderful company, only a good one at a fair price. I'm down 1.94% after 91 days, which means nothing to me, and I'll hold the position as is until the facts say otherwise.

exit_trigger: Loss of or material reduction in a key Navy submarine program; Evidence of management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Sustained decline in ROE below 12% without a clear cause; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting
rationale: I own this one, and nine days in I have no reason to do anything but sit still. General Dynamics builds submarines, combat vehicles and Gulfstream jets, and its moat is largely regulatory: a handful of customers, a handful of shipyards, and clearances and facilities that a newcomer cannot assemble. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 17.2% and debt-to-equity of 0.32, and my owner-earnings DCF gives about $417 a share against $354, a margin of safety of about 15.1%. That clears my 15% bar only barely, so this is a position to keep rather than one to pile into. Government budgets can swing and the submarine and shipyard business runs on thin margins, and the snapshot gives me no figures on earnings consistency, CEO tenure, or insider activity, so my confidence is moderate. I'll hold and let time work.

exit_trigger: Evidence of moat erosion, such as sustained loss of pricing power or volume to private label; Management destroying value through large, poorly priced acquisitions; Discovery that reported leverage is materially understated versus the filing; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value on a persistent basis; Verified failure of the ten-year earnings consistency test
rationale: I own this one, and nothing in the numbers in front of me gives me a reason to change that. Soup and snacks are a business I can explain in two paragraphs, and the figures I can see are good: a five-year average ROE of 21.66%, debt-to-equity of 0.10, and owner earnings averaging about $829 million against a market cap of about $6.78 billion. The snapshot's intrinsic value of $43.71 a share, built on zero growth and a 5% discount rate, against a $22.76 price leaves a margin of 47.93%. That is more cushion than I require, but I want to be honest about what I cannot check here. The ten-year earnings record, CEO tenure and the return on invested capital are not in the snapshot, and a debt ratio that low for a packaged-food company deserves a look at the filing. Packaged-food brands face pressure from private label and changing tastes, so I will keep the position at its current size, not add, until the missing pieces are confirmed.

exit_trigger: Evidence of lasting price competition from online distributors eroding gross margins; Sustained decline in ROE below 15% without a clear cause; Management makes a large value-destroying acquisition or shows dishonesty; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value persistently
rationale: I own this one, and I bought it only eleven days ago at $120.05; it now trades at $112.65, down 6.16%. A price drop with the business unchanged does not bother me. It is the sort of thing I would want to see, because the margin of safety is now 28.3% against my 15% minimum. The snapshot shows 5-year average ROE of 20.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.35, and owner earnings averaging about $303 million, which is a respectable profile for a distributor of industrial supplies that competes on scale, breadth of inventory and service. I will keep the shares and not add yet. The snapshot says nothing about CEO tenure, insider activity, 10-year earnings consistency or the actual moat metrics, and the 5% discount rate and 8% growth cap are assumptions I should not lean on too hard. If those gaps check out, I would be happy to own more at lower prices.

rationale: I own this one, and two weeks in I have no reason to do anything but sit. A.O. I cannot check ten years of earnings, CEO tenure, or the ROIC from this snapshot, so my confidence stays moderate rather than high.
